caption_en: 47. Room (11), S wall: black plinth (?); middle area with red central panel containing an vanid picture and yellow side panels; discolored upper area.

48. Room (12), N wall: remains of a fresco with a black plinth and a middle area with a red central panel and yellow side panels. In the center of the wall is the painting reproduced in the following figures.
49. Room (12), N wall: the remains of the painting interpreted by Helbig (H, 1382) as the delivery of arms to Aeneas by Aphrodite.

50. Room (12): drawing by G. Marsigli of the painting reproduced in the previous figure. It is probable that it is the same painting erroneously indicated by Bechi (Bechi 1835, p. 5) as depicting Ulysses who "shows in Scyros to Achilles concealed in feminine robes the weapons in order to recognize him among those damsels", to which corresponds in Helbig's catalog no. 1303, given as lost, which should therefore be considered a reduplication of no. 1382 and expunged. Moreover, Helbig already thought that his number 1290, given up by him for lost, could perhaps be a reduplication of 1382, the only one of the three paintings discussed here that he actually saw.
51. Vestibule (14) of entrance no. 5: cocciopesto floor decorated with a dotted with large white tiles, dating back to the Republican age.  79 N56155

53. Room (15), N wall: the room was equipped with a staircase, the imprint of which remains in the plaster, which led to a mezzanine of which the holes are recognizable to insert the beams that supported the floor; you can see the cocciopesto floor dotted with white tiles.
52. Vestibule (14), S wall, with opus incertum masonry and limestone block heads and fresco remains, now illegible, which contained plants and birds in the plinth.

54. Peristyle (16), E wall, S section: on the left is the pilaster covered with white fluted stucco that flanked the tablinum (26); On the right is the door to the room (28), with a discharge arch made of small limestone blocks. The paintings, now completely vanished, are assigned to the III style by Mau (Mau W, p. 420).
55. Room (17), N wall, central section: detail of the faded upper area, containing an aedicule flanked by arched garlands. III style. 79 N56159
56. Triclinium (18), S-E corner: remains of the cocciopesto floor.   79 N56157

57. Triclinium (18), N wall with remains of a fresco of the III style: the plinth is black; of the middle area only the scheme formed by a central aedicule flanked by panels can be recognized; the upper area is discolored.
58. Triclinium (18), S-W corner with remains of a fresco of the III style. 79 N56143

59. Triclinium (20): of the decoration of the vast room in the S-W corner of the house, only this panel remains, which reproduces a black monochrome wall. In the plinth are three compartments with birds; in the center of the middle area is a structure similar to that witnessed in houses VI 2, 14 and IX 1, 22: a crossing of garlands with a small medallion in the center; in the side panels are two plant motifs. The upper area is occupied by a light aedicule structure (cf. the House of Trebius Valens III 2, 1, vol. III, p. 367, fig. 39), in the centre of which an eagle with spread wings holds a small picture with animals. The two friezes of lotuses and palmettes executed in a very cursive manner are a characteristic motif of the last phase of the III style. The table reproduced here, which in the nineteenth-century bibliography refers to this room, is instead referred to the nearby cubicle (18) by Bastet (cited in the bibl.). from Zahn II, Tav. '74 (Fot. Rossini)
60. Triclinium (20), N-E corner. 79 N56147
61. Triclinium (20), S wall: the wall is perhaps the same as the decoration reproduced in fig. 59, but of which nothing remains.

62. Room (24): the old photograph reproduces the floor with a motif consisting of white squares with black crosses and black squares with white crosses, alternating with hourglasses, datable to the II style (for an identical, and contemporary, redaction of the motif see vol. I, House I 6, 2, p. 230, fig. 64, with central emblem removed in antiquity; PRoma, p. 178, fig. 40). DAIR 72.768
63. Wardrobe (25), with window with marble sill and remains of frescoes, now illegible.

64. Tablinum (26), floor: in the carpet of black tesserae are scattered marble tiles and slabs; the central emblem is also made of square marble tiles, bordered by a motif of overlapping triangles; black and white bands run along the walls of the room. The floor, dating back to the imperial age, is the later of those preserved in the house.

65. Tablinum (26), N wall: above the black plinth (?) with plants, the middle area has red side panels, while the centre of the wall contained an aedicule with a yellow background in which was the painting with Meleager and Atalanta (see fig. below). The wall can be assigned to the final phase of the III style, and its decoration included "a black frieze in which there are fauns and bacchantes in various attitudes" (Bechi 1835, p. 7). 79 N56129

66. Tablinum (26): from the centre of the N wall comes the painting now in the National Museum of Naples (inv. 8980; H, 1165), in which, in a large-format version, the hunter Meleager is depicted, in the company of Atalanta and two companions (the uncles who contend with Atalanta for the remains of the Calydonian boar?, cf. LIMC II, pp. 943, n. 34; 949). Diap. AFSN 30466

67. Tablinum (26), overlooking the rear garden through a large and wide window with a marble sill, winged of which are two small niches painted on a blue background. The wall has a black base, yellow predellas and a red middle area.

68. Tablinum (26): in the center of the S wall was the painting from which the modern name given to the house derives. It depicts Heracles and Deianira (sister of Meleager, represented in the painting on the opposite wall, see fig. 66) who arrived with their son Illus at the river Eveno, where the centaur Nessus, ferrying Heracles' wife, would have fallen in love with her, provoking the wrath of the hero who kills him (H, 1146; MNN, inv. 9001). The composition, of which four other contemporary replicas are known by Pompe (cf. vol. I, House I 7, 19, p. 77, fig. 49), is characterized by the contrast between the brown complexion of the male bodies in the foreground — with some details rendered in a rather unfortunate way — and the light background given by the landscape element, in which the figure of Deianira stands out on the chariot. Diap. AFSN 30465

69. Triclinium (27): from this room comes the large circular emblem, now in the National Museum of Naples (inv. 10019), depicting a lion hunted by cupids in front of two Maenads and a statue of Dionysus, which has been attributed to the same workshop active in the House of the Faun, VI 12, 2 (cf. Meyboom Meded 1977, p. 72, notes 272, 273; p. 74, note 287). AFSN A5898

70. Triclinium (27): Zahn's panel, which has a narrow compartment on a dark red background with decorative motifs typical of the late III style, allows us to get an idea of the decoration of this room, in which it was evidently decided to renew only the wall covering, while maintaining the older and more complex floor decoration (see previous fig.).  from Zahn II, Tav. 59 (Fot. Rossini)

70. Triclinium (27): Zahn's panel, which has a narrow compartment on a dark red background with decorative motifs typical of the late III style, allows us to get an idea of the decoration of this room, in which it was evidently decided to renew only the wall covering, while maintaining the older and more complex floor decoration (see previous fig.).  from Zahn II, Tav. 59 (Fot. Rossini)
71. Triclinium (27), S wall with remains of a fresco of the III style. 79 N56128

72. Fauces (28): the floor of the room that connects the Corinthian atrium (16) and the garden (29) is made of cocciopesto with a small dotting of white tiles, datable to the Republican age. 79 N56139
73. Fauces (28), S wall: remains of a fresco of the third style with a black plinth, red middle and upper areas. The same decoration is located on the wall in front.

74. Fauces (28), S wall, section E: the detail of the black geometric plinth with a cross motif typical of the III style allows us to verify the reliability of the nineteenth-century descriptions (Overbeck P 4, p. 334) that assign the decoration reproduced here to this phase.

75. Triclinium (32): the room, open onto the large garden (29) and today very difficult to reach due to the collapse of the vaults of the service rooms below, has a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with a rather irregular course and a border with a high black band. The characteristic arrangement of the tesserae (quasi reticulatum in the definition of Pernice, p. 45, who notes that it is later than the wall decorations of the first style, now almost completely lost: see the following fig.)

76. Triclinium (32): the drawing published in the Bourbon Museum presents, above an unindicated plinth, a scan of the wall in orthostats marked by pilasters and surmounted by a Doric frieze. The stucco cladding of the first style was animated by polychromy ("stuccoes painted in various colors of marble", Bechi 1835, p.8). from MB VI, Tav. AB (Fot. Rossini)

1. The façade on the Via di Mercurio, with opus incertum masonry covered with white stucco, imitating a wall of marble blocks, above a paneled plinth. The door of entrance 6 has the typical appearance of the portals of the Republican age, flanked by high tuff pilasters that support square, cubic capitals, whose limited protrusion with respect to the pilasters is probably due to later alterations. The small windows correspond to the rooms on the ground floor, while the larger openings gave light to the rooms on the upper floor or to rooms on the ground floor with higher ceilings.

2. Façade on the Via di Mercurio with stucco cladding in imitation of the opus quadratum. According to Bechi (MB V, p. 3), the plinth was red, and the carvings that delimit the ashlars were underlined by a blue color.

3. S-shaped façade of entrance no. 6: the stucco opus quadratum imitates and takes up the "model" of the severe stucco coverings of the first style datable to the Republican age, but the frame with impressed motifs reveals its seriousness and allows this covering to be dated to the period of the fourth style.

4. The "architectural" aspect of the cladding of this façade aroused the interest of the architect Pasquale Maria Veneri (the watercolour is dated 1843), to whom we owe other reproductions of stucco coverings in imitation of masonry structures. The high plinth, now completely discolored, was purple orthostats.  ADS 327 (Fot. Pedicini)
5. S-shaped façade of entrance 6: the stucco cladding was concluded at the top by a frame of lotuses and palmettes, similar to those usual on walls of the fourth style.

6. S-shaped façade of entrance 7, constituting the S-W corner of the insula: the masonry is here in opus reticulatum with brick adhesions, in which the cubic tuff capital dating back to the Republican age is inserted. The stucco opus quadratum cladding is coeval with that covering the façade of entrance no. 6 and masks the differences in masonry technique between the two complexes.

7. S-shaped façade of entrance no. 7: opus reticulatum masonry with brick adhesions and stucco ashlar cladding. The two "loopholes" correspond to the rooms on the upper floor. On the right, near the edge of the insula, you can see the closure of a "bridge hole", intended for fixing the scaffolding. 78 N46829
8. S façade of entrance no. 7: stucco frame with a typical motif of the IV style, lotuses and palmettes.  78 N46817

9. The decoration of the façade, combined with the figuration of Mercury that adorned the pilaster S (H, 18), had suggested to the nineteenth-century excavators the idea of recognizing in this building a Collegium Mercatorum (PAH II, p. 205), an idea they themselves abandoned (ibid., p. 208) as the continuation of the excavation did not offer other elements to support this hypothesis. The god, here accompanied by Fortuna, is in fact frequently represented on the facades of houses, as a wish for profit.
10. Cross-section (E-W) with the relief of the painted decorations, from anonymous nineteenth-century watercolor. In the center is the aedicule of the viridarium (45).
11. Longitudinal section (N-S): in the center is the impluvium of the Tuscan atrium of entrance no. 77.  from PParigi, fig. 81 (Fot. Rossini) 867

12. Vestibule (33), wall N. From the entrance, from the large vestibule with a marble threshold, the important "tone" of the decoration of this house is announced. On the high red plinth are panels with plants; the middle area has a red central panel with a removed central motif (see figs. 14-15) and yellow side panels: the upper area, also red, probably contained two low squares, now unrecognizable. A pilaster covered with fluted stucco, red in the lower part and white in the upper part, marks the entrance to the atrium. IV style.

13. Vestibule (33), S wall: the decorative scheme is identical to that of the wall in front (see fig. above). The central motif has also been detached from this wall (see figs. 1415). IV style. The door gives access to the cubicle (34), whose walls are covered only with a high plinth of cocciopesto.  78 N46780

14. Vestibule (33); on the red background of the middle area, distributed like fendants on the two walls of the vestibule, the figures of the Dioscuri (H, 963) stood and covered only by the chlamys, while holding the horses by the bridle. On the head of each of the twins is the star of Zeus, which rests on the pileus, symbol of the eggs from which they were born and which Leda conceived by Zeus who turned into a swan (MNN, inv. no. 9453).
15. Vestibule (33): the vignette depicting one of the two Dioscuri (MNN, inv. no. 9455), which faced the one reproduced in the previous figure, clumsily imitated here.  Diap. AFSN 30471
17. Cubicle (B), wall E with recessed bed: black plinth with plants; Middle area with black central compartment and red side panels. IV style.

16. Cubicle (B), N wall: the small room, overlooking the atrium, has recessed bed recesses on the side walls, while the back wall retains the lunette. The wall decoration, very simple and "poor" compared to that of other rooms in the same house, has not been protected and has almost completely vanished. The short wall — as often happens in cubicles of the fourth style — is divided into two parts by a narrow central compartment with a white background, on the side of which are red panels. In the black plinth are compartments with plants; the upper area and the bezel are white.
19. Cubicle (B), wall S: the geometric designs were engraved with a compass on the still fresh plaster of the central compartment not to serve as a guide for the decorator, but as a pastime.
18. Cubicle (B), wall S: the space on the wall in front (see fig. 16) containing the red side panel is here occupied by the door leading to the atrium (37). IV style.

20. Laconic (F): a remnant of a mosaic floor with a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, a border with a black band and a high marginal flounce of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp.

21. Laconic (F), wall E. The room was covered by a false lowered vault: the four walls preserve the remains of a decoration with a middle area with black panels and a stucco frame, datable to the fourth style.

22. Cubicle (35), floor of the antechamber: on the background of cocciopesto are scattered numerous flakes of travertine and some of colored limestone, which suggest a dating to the Republican age, at the time of the first style. On the left you can see the similar floor of the alcove, slightly raised. The distinction between the part intended for the bed and the antechamber, emphasized by the structure of the floor decoration, is instead abolished in the later wall decoration of the fourth style, which treats unitary and with the same

23. Cubicle (35), N wall: the overall view allows us to appreciate the richness and meticulousness of the wall decoration of the IV style with a white background, characterized by the deities depicted within thòloi on the three walls, in the center of the upper area. The skeleton of the decoration is given — as in the cubicle (B) (see fig. 16) — by a bipartite structure, here, however, hardly recognizable by the overabundance of decorative elements, moreover of unequal quality.
25. Cubicle (35), wall N, section O: the wall is perceived as a space to be decorated with imagination, outside any "structural" logic, as is evident in this detail
24. Cubicle (35), N wall, section W: the side panel of the middle area supports two "acroterial" dolphins; in the center is an eagle on a globe with spread wings. IV style.

27. Cubicle (35), N wall, central section: above the candelabrum reproduced in the previous figure, within an aedicule with a shell-shaped basin, a peacock is represented doing the wheel, above which is a sphinx. IV style.

26. Cubicle (35), N wall, central section: the architectural view is occupied by a slender vegetable candelabrum, with birds and masks that can be glimpsed hanging, made with considerable decorative detail, which contrasts with the very rapid execution of the sphinx that supports the candelabrum itself. IV style.
29. Cubicle (35), wall E, section S: in the centre of the panel of the middle area, framed by a stretched garland, is a figure of an offerer, rendered with sharply engraved outlines.

28. Cubicle (35), N wall, central section: the goddess (Aphrodite ?) in the centre of the upper area is made, like all the figures in this room, with the help of rapid graffiti contour lines, which the fall of the overpainted colour has made visible again.
30. Cubicle (35), S wall, section E: detail of the upper area, with scenography and draped figure. IV style. 78 N46443
31. Cubicle (35), S wall: the decoration is symmetrical to that of the N wall. A] above the red plinth (not framed), the white middle area has a foreshortening in the center
32. Cubicle (35), S wall, section E: white upper area with birds on a plant candelabra and tree within architecture. IV style.
33. Cubicle (35), S wall: in the centre of the upper area, within a leafy pergola, Hera is depicted enthroned, with a sceptre in her left hand, above which an eagle flies. IV style. 78 N46441
34. Cubicle (35), S wall, section O: the decoration is symmetrical to that of fig. 32, but here the lower part of a human figure is preserved above the vegetable candelabrum. IV style.

35. Cubicle (35), W wall, with a splayed window overlooking the Way of Mercury. It is the best-preserved wall in the room, which allows you to evaluate the amount of decorative elements present in the decoration. Also in the center of this wall, in the upper area, there is a figure of a deity.

36. Cubicle (35), O wall, section S: vignette with figure on a shelf in the centre of the panel, framed by stretched garlands, on which, like acroteria, sea monsters supporting cornucopias rest. On the top of the panel there is a small picture with a blue background depicting a landscape with architecture, on which a vase and two swans holding garlands in their beaks are still resting. IV style.

37. Cubicle (35), O wall, S section: detail of the previous figure. The landscape picture belongs to a very popular genre on the walls of Pompeii, which manages to vary infinitely a series of basic elements (porticoed buildings, views of seascapes, boats and human figures), obtaining always different and pleasing results. IV style.
38. Cubicle (35), O wall, section S: detail of the landscape picture in the previous figure. IV style.
39. Cubicle (35), O wall, section S, detail of fig. 35: white upper area with a draped and crowned figure overlooking a light architectural structure. IV style.
40. Cubicle (35), W wall, central section: architectural view with candelabrum.

41. Cubicle (35), wall W: in the centre of the upper area Poseidon with the trident in his left hand and his right leg resting on a rock, in the scheme attributed to the statue of the god created by Lysippus for Corinth. IV style.

43. Cubicle (35), W wall, section N: upper white area with a draped figure overlooking a "scenography" on which a winged figure with a body ending in scrolls and a goat are depicted as acroteria. IV style.
42. Cubicle (35), O wall, section N: in the centre of the white panel framed by taut garlands in the middle area is a figure on a corbel, built with sure, deeply engraved lines. IV style.
44. Cubicle (35): the decorative exuberance does not overlook the jambs of the splayed window on wall O, also painted, like the rest of the room, in the fourth style with a white background.
45. Cubicle (35), N jamb of the window, with bird resting on a plant shoot.

46. Atrium (37), view from NE. The fluted tuff columns are covered with two layers of white stucco with grooves. The state of conservation of the paintings, partly detached and partly completely vanished, prevents us from perceiving the richness of the decoration, based on a grandiose scheme of the IV style, in which a large part was reserved for figures of divinities. In the atrium the excavators could also recognize "the traces of mobile paintings of the ancients embedded in the wall, but which no longer exist at present" (PAH II, p. 208).

47. Atrium (37): at the bottom of the large tuff impluvium, with mouldings dating back to the Republican age, marble tiles of various types and shapes were subsequently inserted to enrich and modernize it, bedded in cocciopesto, whose polychromy does not accord with the simplicity of the oldest decoration.
48. Atrium (37): in the centre of the E side of the impluvium, in axis with the vestibule, is a base for a statue covered in marble.
49. Atrium (37): well curb grooved in travertine to draw water from the cistern below the impluvium.

50. Entrance hall (37), Entrance wall (39) and (40). At the base of masonry covered with marble was secured the safe, about which we read in PAH II, p. 214: "On the 8th of July a wooden chest was found fixed with a factory in the ground, embellished with meanders, foliage, bas-reliefs, and all sorts of bronze ornaments, which served it elegantly as a fortress and decoration. a great damage to the arts and archaeology, not to have taken from my predecessor a drawing, or made a description of this unique monument of antiquity. I have scarcely come to see the remnants of it, piled up in various corners, and to groan over so much ruin. In this chest were found 45 gold coins (as far as I have been told, imperial), and 5 silver coins" (cf. also PAH III, p. 89). The coffin had been partly searched by ancient prospectors (MB V, p. 7). On the N wall of the atrium was the vignette with Ares described in H, 273, which is no longer recognizable today. 78 N46471

51. Atrium (37), S wall, section E: the section of the atrium between the door of the oecus (43) and the passage to the peristyle (53) was decorated, above the red plinth, with a yellow panel (left) and a red panel (right), which contained a tall vignette with Nike in flight bearing a shield on which were inscribed the letters S(enatus) C(onsulto) (H,  909), now completely vanished. In the right-hand corner of the door (43), there are remains of a painted decoration underneath that of the IV style, datable (according to Overbeck P4, p. 335) to the III style.

52. Atrium (37): on the S side of the atrium there is a large passage to the peristyle (53), framed by high pilasters covered with red and white stucco crossed by grooves. The hoof was dark red with plants; the middle area was also red, which contained, on the left (between the pilaster and the door) a torn vignette (see fig. below). In the upper area, also red, there were paintings with mythological landscapes, now lost, depicting Europa on the bull (H, 1530) and Andromeda freed by Perseus (H, 1203).
53. Atrium (37); vignette with Saturn cloaked, with a sickle in his right hand (H, 96; MNN, inv. 8837), which was located to the left of the gate of (D).

54. Atrium(37), S side: from the left of the passage leading to the peristyle comes the vignette with Apollo Citaredo, with a nimbus and laurel wreath on his head, with his left foot resting on the base of an archaistic female statue (H, 181). The fragment, donated to Sir William Temple, ambassador in Naples, by Ferdinand II of Bourbon, is now in the British Museum.  Photos. Brit. Mus.

55. Atrium (37), S side, on the right, i.e. W of the passage to the peristyle (53): the plinth is red with plants; from the middle area, also red, the vignette reproduced in fig. 56 was torn out, above which Europa was depicted kidnapped by the bull; in the upper area, above the passage, there was a large painting with Pan and Hermaphrodite (see fig. 57).

56. Atrium (37), vignette with standing Ceres, with a basket of spies in the left hand and torch in the right (H, 176; MNN, inv. 9454), coming from the stretch of wall to the right of the passage to the peristyle (53). Diap. AFSN 30470
57. Atrium (37): painting with Pan portraying himself before Hermaphrodite discovering his sex (H, 1870; MNN, inv. 2'7700), which was located above the door leading to the peristyle (53).
58. Atrium (37), S side with the door of (E). Remains of fresco of the fourth style: in the upper area you can recognize the traces of a painting, which must have contained a landscape.
59. Atrium (37), S wall near the S-W corner: above the red plinth, in the red and yellow panels of the middle area, there were two vignettes (see fig. 60). IV style.

60. Atrium (37): from the W section of the $S wall comes the vignette with Dionysus and Satyr (H, 400; MNN, inv. 9268): in the centre, much higher than the figures on either side of him, is the standing god, with thyrsus in his left hand and a kantharos in his lower right, from which a young Satyr drinks; on the right is the panther, sacred to the god.

61. Atrium (37), wall OaN of the vestibule (33): the pilaster on the left marks the passage between the atrium and the vestibule. The symmetrical wall, to the S of the vestibule, contained a representation of Fortuna with the cornucopia and the rudder resting on the globe, now lost: based on Helbig's description (H, 942), one might think that it is the same vignette reproduced here in fig. 9.

62. Atrium (37): from one of the walls of the room comes the "very fond" vignette representing Zeus enthroned crowned by a Victory; at his feet are the "cosmic" symbols of the eagle and the globe (H, 102; MNN, inv. 9551). AFSN 30472

63. Triclinium (38), N wall: red panelled plinth, white middle area with panels separated by architectural views; white upper area with architecture. In the center of the wall is the gap left by the tearing of the painting (see figure 65). IV style.

64. 'Triclinio (38), wall E: even on this wall the decoration is almost completely vanished; In the center of the wall was a painting, also apparently detached, but not identified. IV style.  78 N46418

65. Triclinium (38), wall N: the painting with Endymion reached by Selene, which was in the center of the wall, now in the National Museum of Naples (inv. 9240; H, 960). On the left is seated the hunter accompanied by his dog; Selene descends towards him, while in the background two figures embrace, frightened by the celestial apparition.

66. Triclinium (38), S wall: the plaster, almost completely collapsed, however retains its colours better than the wall in front. In the red plinth is a narrow compartment with a bird in flight; in the side panel, between stretched garlands and carpet edges, is a Medusa head. IV style.

67. Triclinium (38), W wall: the red plinth is divided into panels containing dolphins (in the centre) and deer (on the sides), and in narrow compartments containing drinking horns (rhytà). In the center of the white middle area is a panel that contained a painting depicting Narcissus, completely vanished (see next figure) between two large architectural views; The upper area is also white, with architecture. IV style.

68. The painting with Narcissus, in the company of a Nymph (Echo?), a cupid and the dog (H, 1364), left in situ unprotected in the centre of the W wall of the triclinium (38), has completely vanished and is documented only by nineteenth-century descriptions and reproductions (this is taken from MB I, fig. 4). The same subject, in a different iconography, had also been chosen to decorate the walls of the triclinium (49) (see fig. 179) and is also lost.

69. Cubicle (39), floor. The room, in the centre of the N side of the Corinthian atrium (37), retains a floor dating back to the second style, in which the polychromy of the tesserae gives relief and depth to the edge, which alternates swastika meanders and squares. The central mat and the high border are made up of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp.
70. Cubicle (39), floor: detail of the polychrome mosaic border.
71. Cubicle (39), SE corner: marble threshold with two recesses in correspondence with a wardrobe or a walled-in door.

72. Cubicle (39), wall N. The decoration of the walls has been renewed and is more recent (IV style) (and much more common) than the flooring. The hoof is black, with plants; the middle area has a black central panel and red side panels; in the center of the panels were small squares now completely vanished. IV style.
73. Cubicle (39), wall E: black plinth with plants; middle area with red central panel and black side panel. IV style.
74. Cubicle (39), O wall:
76. Fauces (41), parete N:

75. Wing (40), N wall with limestone block masonry, covered by now illegible remains of frescoes, datable, according to Overbeck (Overbeck P4, pp. 336-337) and Mau (Mau W, p. 258) to the II style and preserved because they were protected by a wardrobe. A safe was attached to the lava base (another ark base is in fig. 50), to be identified with the one described in PAH II, pp. 214-215: "A '19 detto" (July 1828) "another chest similar to the previous one was discovered, but smaller and less elegant, and was collected among many pieces of bronze and iron decorations,  a lock with a simple padlock, a bas-relief representing a dog flattened in the bottom of the minted chest, and a bust of a deity, perhaps of a Fortune, who had the casket in custody, and which must have been located in the middle of its cover on the inside".
77. Tablinum (42), floor: detail of the high marginal flounce of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp.
78. Tablinum (42): in the centre of the floor there is a flap of the carpet of small white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp.

Picture with Medea who, in revenge for Jason's abandonment, meditates the killing of their children (H, 1262, MNN, inv. 8977): in her left hand she hides her sword, while she observes her children playing unaware; on the left the old pedagogue comes out of a door. Psychological research seems to take over here, in the anguish expressed by Medea's large wide eyes, while the calm in which the children are immersed emphasizes even more the impending drama, reflected in the face of the old pedagogue. The architectural setting, on the other hand, is reduced to the essentials and the large background behind Medea contains only a quickly built portico.

49. The predella now in the National Museum of Naples (inv. 9219) with a cupid who has freed a dog against a wild boar that is about to bite into an apple, probably comes from wall E of this room, although reproduced by Zahn below the painting with Zephyr and Chloris.

50. Garden (27): the portico erected only on the southern side, with pillars covered with fluted stucco and with Corinthian capitals, leans against the wall in opus quadrata pertaining to the first construction phase of the house. AFS A136 (formerly A7283)

1. Southern façade in Vicolo di Mercurio from W. In the foreground, the S-W corner of the house with repairs after 62 AD. To the E is the access to the secondary atrium (3), a restored crack in the wall at the outer corner of the tetrastyle atrium building and the access to the latter.

2. Entrance 9 with vestibule and atrium fauces (3). The lava threshold belongs to the construction phase of about 150 BC while the capitals of the cubic tuff pilasters, unfinished, were added during 1 restoration carried out around the year 100 BC.

3. S-E corner of the house: on the left the Alley of Mercury, on the right the Alley of the Labyrinth. After the earthquake of 62 AD, the entire corner of the house was repaired in opus testaceum with adhesions filled with mesh in the most recent opus incertum.

4. Original entrance to the hortus to the E with architrave and fence in square blocks of Sarno limestone. On the occasion of the construction of the peristyle (36) (after 100 BC) the gate was walled up. Inside, the wall was divided into two parts by a stucco pilaster.  DAIB 79.2.093 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

5. SideOof the house on Pan's Alley. You can see the difference between the plinth of the wall in opus incertum of lava and the overlying masonry in opus incertum of limestone mixed with cruma. Where plaster cladding is lacking, horizontal worktops are visible at irregular intervals.

6. Room (2), S-E corner. Leaning against the wall S is the podium for the wooden staircase leading to a mezzanine, the height of which is indicated by two holes for beams. On the pergula are 1-2 beds for slaves, below it a warehouse for amphorae.

7. Room (2), NW corner. Located next to the fauces (1), room (2) served not only as a pantry and lodging for slaves, but also as an entrance to a vaulted cellar. The staircase descends along the W wall from S to N. AdE of the entrance is a built-in wardrobe.

8. The staircase leading to the cellar, clogged with lapilli and fragments of tiles, was discovered only in 1980 during the cleaning of the floor of the room (2). The compartment is 79 cm wide and 2.58 m long. On three sides of the entrance is a recess for the wooden frame of the trapdoor.

9. N-W corner of the vaulted cellar (2 A). At the ninth and last step of the staircase is an interruption after which the flight bends to an E. The deep cracks in the wall plaster were probably caused by the earthquake of 62 AD.

10. Cellar (2A), view of the S-E part. The cellar is covered by a barrel vault with a N-S direction, 1.75 m wide and 2.30 m high. The length is 2.96 m on the E side and 3.06 m on the W side. At a height of about 0.5 m from the floor level, three semicircular niches open on both longitudinal walls, 40-50 cm deep. At the time of its discovery in 1980, apart from the lapilli from which it had been filled, the cellar contained no other materials. It was probably originally used for the preservation of foodstuffs in the cool; it seems, however, that after the earthquake of 62 A.D. it was no longer used.

11. Travertine threshold between the cubicle (29) and the atrium (3) (1.58 x 0.52 m). The trapezoidal recesses are common to all the thresholds set up during the renovation of the house in the 70s and 60s BC. They were equipped with wooden elements on which the side frames, also wooden, of the doors were nailed. At the front the door frame was fixed in a groove.

12. Atriotuscanico (3), view of the S$ side, with entrance no. 9. The atrium measures 10.88 m, from Na S, and 7.92 m from O to E. On the left is the doorway that leads into the room (2), in the center the vestibulum and the fauces (1), on the right the entrances to the corridor (4) and to the room (6). At the front is the tuff impluvium (internal measurements 2.08 x 1.55 m) and the remains of a brick podium. The floor was in signino, while on the walls, until a hundred years ago, frescoes of the second style were preserved in good condition. DAIB 78.2.099 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

13. Atriotuscanico (3), view of the W side. From the left corridor (4), living room (6), wing (7), servant room (8) and passage leading to the staircase (9). The wing was decorated with remarkable frescoes of the second style, now completely discolored.

14. Atriotuscanico (3), view of the N. In the background, on the left, the passage leading into the courtyard (10) and a view through the window of the exedra (38), opening onto the West portico of the peristyle (36).

15. Atriotuscanico (3), view towards E. On the left you can see the large window of the wing (31) with part of the masonry (restored) after 62 AD. This is followed by the doors of the passage (48), built in the years 70-60 BC and the cubicle (29). It is not possible to establish what the original connection between the two atria was.
16. Corridor (4), O. Cocciopesto floor with scattered fragments of travertine. In all likelihood, the floor is coeval with the decorations of the second style.

17. Odel wall corridor (4) with broken window opening, whose splayed sill is located at a height of 2.50 m. On the left, it is access to the environment (5); on the right, on the opposite side, there is the door of the room (6), walled up after 62 AD. The decoration in the second style has been almost totally lost. The remains of a stucco frame, at the top, and a pilaster, on the right, can be recognized.

18. Wall W of the room (5), preserved up to a height of 5.10 m, with the remains of an oculus with a horizontal diameter of 1.50 m. From its lower part there is a vertical crack caused by the earthquake and repaired with bricks. The plaster was painted with frescoes of the second style, now completely discolored.
